structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, which shaped his tendency to become a confidant for others’ intimate revelations and later led to his disillusionment after returning from the East, except for Gatsby, whom he admires for his extraordinary gift for hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick moves alone to West Egg to learn the bond business, renting a modest eighty-dollar bungalow next to the mysterious Jay Gatsby’s lavish mansion; he feels isolated until a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village, giving him a fleeting sense of belonging. That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, where he meets Daisy and her friend Jordan Baker in their grand Georgian Colonial mansion filled with billowing curtains and cocktails; Tom expresses condescension toward Nick’s profession and later espouses racist pseudoscience from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' while Daisy echoes his views with ironic detachment. A telephone call from New York reveals Tom’s affair, and Daisy confides in Nick that she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool,' exposing her cynicism. After leaving the Buchanans’, Nick returns to his estate by car and sits on an abandoned grass roller in his yard, where he sees Gatsby standing alone on the lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light at the end of a dock, trembling with emotion before vanishing into the night without speaking.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway accompanies Tom Buchanan by train from West Egg to the valley of ashes, a desolate industrial wasteland marked by the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg; Tom forcibly stops the train and introduces Nick to Myrtle Wilson, his mistress, who lives with her husband George B. Wilson at a dilapidated garage. Tom and Myrtle arrange to meet in New York, taking separate train cars to avoid detection, and Myrtle purchases an Airedale puppy, cold cream, perfume, and magazines at the station before boarding a lavender taxicab to a cramped, cluttered apartment on the top floor of a building at 158th Street. There, she hosts a gathering with her sister Catherine and the McKees, during which heavy drinking leads Myrtle to become dramatically theatrical, fantasizing about escaping her husband and marrying Tom, until she dares to shout Daisy’s name—provoking Tom to violently break her nose with his open hand, triggering chaos as women scramble to help, blood stains towels, and Mr. McKee departs silently; Nick leaves with McKee in the elevator and later awakens alone in Pennsylvania Station at dawn, reading the Tribune.

structure.title: III
characters_present: The unnamed driver in the coupé
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation to attend one of Jay Gatsby’s extravagant Saturday evening parties at his Long Island mansion, where guests arrive by Rolls-Royce and station wagon from New York amid orchestras, catered feasts, and five crates of weekly fruit deliveries. Amid drunken rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway meets Jordan Baker and observes surreal details like a butler-operated juicer, a brass bar stocked with forgotten cordials, and a library of genuine books that astonish a drunken guest, Owl Eyes, who insists they are not cardboard props. Gatsby himself remains unseen until late in the night, when he unexpectedly approaches Nick Carraway, offering a polite, charismatic presence and inviting him to fly in his hydroplane the next morning; as the party descends into chaos—champagne-fueled tears, marital fights, and a coupé crashing into a wall with a man still inside—Nick Carraway watches Gatsby stand apart, sober and detached, before bidding farewell on the porch under a faint moon. The chapter shifts to Nick Carraway’s reflections on his daily life in New York, where he works at the Probity Trust, lanches with clerks, studies investments at the Yale Club library, and walks home along Madison Avenue, fantasizing about strangers while sensing a shared loneliness among young office workers; he reconnects with Jordan Baker, initially drawn by her fame as a golf champion, but becomes disillusioned upon learning of her dishonesty—lying about damaging a borrowed car and having moved a golf ball during a tournament—leading him to conclude that he is one of the few honest people he knows.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into chaotic revelry as a vast, name-dropping crowd arrives by car from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, treating him with casual familiarity despite knowing nothing of his past; rumors swirl that he killed a man or is related to Von Hindenburg and the devil. Later, Gatsby picks up Nick in his cream-colored car with nickel accents and a three-noted horn, revealing an elaborate, rehearsed backstory of Oxford education, European aristocratic travels, and wartime heroism—backed by a Montenegrin medal and an Oxford photograph—before hinting that Jordan Baker will speak to Nick about a pending request. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque figure with hair in his nostrils and human molar cuff buttons, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and reveals he fixed the 1919 World Series; Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call and vanishes after Nick introduces him to Tom Buchanan. In a flashback, Jordan recalls meeting Daisy Fay in Louisville in 1917 as she sat in her white roadster with Lieutenant Gatsby, whose romantic gaze she noticed; Daisy later became engaged to Tom Buchanan, married him with extravagant pomp after being found drunk and clutching a letter demanding the $350,000 pearl necklace back, yet wore it the next day. Six weeks prior, Jordan mentioned Gatsby’s name to someone, triggering Daisy’s stunned realization that West Egg’s Gatsby was the same officer from 1917. Finally, in a victoria through Central Park at twilight, Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy, meticulously planning to reconnect through Nick’s house, having spent years reading Chicago newspapers and avoiding direct contact until he felt safe; Nick, moved by Gatsby’s quiet desperation, pulls Jordan closer as he reflects on the emptiness of his own life.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter begins with Nick returning home at night to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but silent, where Gatsby nervously invites him to Coney Island or a swim, then subtly probes his finances and offers a mysterious side business—both of which Nick declines before promising to arrange a tea with Daisy. The next morning, rain falls as Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers; when Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie, Gatsby is visibly shaken, nearly knocking over a clock during their awkward reunion in the living room. After Nick leaves them briefly, he returns to find Daisy tear-stained and Gatsby glowing with quiet joy, now eager to show her his mansion. They walk from the lawn to the house via the road and enter through the big postern, where Daisy admires the estate’s feudal silhouette, gardens filled with jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate, and opulent, eerily empty rooms including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons; Gatsby claims to hear the owl-eyed man laughing ghostly in the library. He then displays his collection of shirts—piled high like bricks in linen, silk, and flannel with stripes, scrolls, plaids, and monograms in coral, apple-green, lavender, and faint orange—causing Daisy to burst into tears over their beauty. As Gatsby watches her with awe, he shows Nick a photograph of Dan Cody and a young picture of himself in yachting attire, which Daisy nostalgically admires; he also displays newspaper clippings about her. Klipspringer is summoned to play piano as thunder rolls over the Sound and lights flicker across West Egg, but his performance is poor yet compelled. Nick attempts to leave but is ignored as Gatsby and Daisy become completely absorbed in each other, with Gatsby grasping Daisy’s hand, moved by her voice, while the green light on her dock, once symbolic, now seems diminished in meaning.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving at Gatsby’s West Egg mansion seeking a statement based on unverified rumors, unaware that Gatsby is not a public figure; this encounter segues into a reflective account of Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht anchored off Lake Superior in a torn green jersey and canvas pants, later spending five years aboard the Tuolomee in roles including steward, mate, skipper, secretary, and jailor, only to be left with nothing but his refined persona after Ella Kaye legally secured Cody’s fortune; weeks later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled by the unexpected arrival of Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit on horseback, who are invited in for drinks but coldly decline supper, revealing their condescension; later that week, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is initially enchanted but grows increasingly appalled by the chaotic energy of West Egg, prompting Gatsby to confide in Nick Carraway his belief that he can repeat the past and restore his lost love with Daisy by having her declare she never loved Tom, so they can return to Louisville as if five years had never passed, while Gatsby stands alone haunted by the memory of kissing Daisy under the moonlight five years prior.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a broiling summer afternoon, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans' house to find Gatsby waiting, having replaced all original servants with silent, suspicious replacements to avoid gossip during Daisy's frequent visits; during lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, shocking Tom, who dismisses Gatsby's claim of attending Oxford as 'Oxford, New Mexico' and insists they go to town, leading to a tense car swap where Tom drives Gatsby’s yellow car while Gatsby takes Tom’s coupé with Daisy. The group stops at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes, where Wilson, visibly ill and emotionally distressed, reveals he plans to move West with Myrtle and asks to sell his car—unaware that Myrtle is having an affair—and Myrtle watches from the window, mistaking Jordan for Tom’s wife in a moment of jealous terror. At the Plaza Hotel in New York, the confrontation escalates as Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and drugstores, forcing Daisy to admit she once loved both men, shattering Gatsby’s idealized vision; Tom orders them to return to Long Island in Gatsby’s car, ending the argument. Later, Myrtle is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car—witnessed by Michaelis, who initially describes it as light green—as she rushes out of the garage after hearing Wilson interrogate him about his whereabouts; Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Wilson in grief-stricken shock, and Tom reassures Wilson he was not driving the yellow car, clarifying his own vehicle is blue. That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby emerges from the shadows to confess Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle but insists he will take the blame; through a pantry window, Nick sees Daisy and Tom sitting together at their kitchen table, sharing food and ale in quiet, intimate silence, revealing their reconciliation, while Gatsby remains outside in the moonlight, standing vigil over her house as if guarding a dream.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after Daisy’s failed visit, Gatsby, emotionally shattered, recounts to Nick Carraway his first meeting with Daisy and his deception to appear her social equal, clinging to the illusion that she never truly loved Tom. Later, in a quiet, fire-lit room before his departure for abroad, Gatsby shares an intimate, wordless moment with Daisy, savoring their connection as it eclipses all his former ambitions. Meanwhile, after returning from the war and being mistakenly sent to Oxford, Gatsby learns of Daisy’s decision to marry Tom Buchanan while receiving letters that reveal her despair amid her opulent, hollow social life. At dawn on Long Island, Gatsby insists their relationship was 'just personal' and recalls his haunting return to Louisville, desperately reaching for the fading memory of Daisy as the city disappears behind him; after breakfast, he reveals he never used his pool all summer. Nick Carraway, reluctant to leave, misses two trains before finally departing, praising Gatsby as worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' met with a radiant smile. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, fixates on the yellow car and interprets the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg as God’s judgment, eventually tracing Gatsby’s name and walking to West Egg. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring any call to the pool, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and orders the damaged car left untouched; he disappears toward the pool, where he is later found dead, floating beside the drifting mattress, moments after Wilson’s body is discovered in the grass — the tragic culmination of his unattainable dream.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left alone to navigate the chaotic aftermath as police, photographers, and curious onlookers swarm his mansion, while media narratives reduce Wilson’s crime to the act of a 'madman' and Catherine denies any connection between Gatsby and Myrtle. Despite desperate efforts—calling Daisy, sending a letter to Meyer Wolfsheim, and waiting for a response—Nick Carraway receives only cold evasions, including Wolfsheim’s telegram citing 'important business' and a mistaken long-distance call that abruptly ends when Gatsby’s death is revealed. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, overwhelmed and exhausted, sharing a worn photograph of Gatsby’s house and a copy of Hopalong Cassidy containing his son’s youthful self-improvement schedule, revealing Gatsby’s humble origins and relentless ambition. Nick Carraway attempts to rally mourners, but nearly all refuse: Klipspringer only asks for his tennis shoes to be mailed, and Wolfsheim avoids him entirely, claiming he never gets involved after a death. At the funeral, only Gatz, a Lutheran minister from Flushing, Nick Carraway, and a few servants are present as rain falls; an unexpected guest, the man with owl-eyed glasses—whom Nick Carraway had met months earlier in Gatsby’s library—appears splashing through the mud, wipes his glasses to view the grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' after a religious phrase, and laments, 'The poor son-of-a-bitch.' Later, Nick Carraway recalls his Middle West as defined by winter train journeys to Chicago, realizing he and his circle—Tom, Daisy, Gatsby, Jordan—were all Westerners fundamentally unfit for the East’s moral decay, symbolized by a haunting El Greco-like vision of West Egg where a drunken woman lies abandoned on a stretcher. He confronts Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man; their bitter exchange over dishonesty and carelessness ends with his quiet resignation. On Fifth Avenue, he encounters Tom Buchanan, who admits he told Wilson that Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary and describing his own emotional breakdown over dog biscuits left in his abandoned flat—a moment Nick finds grotesque but understands as self-justified. After selling his car and packing his trunk, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s empty house one final time at night, erasing a crudely scrawled obscenity from the white steps, then walks to the beach where he watches the ferryboat lights and reflects on Gatsby’s belief in the green light, concluding that the American dream, like Gatsby’s, is a future forever receding as we strive toward it, borne back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves from the Midwest to West Egg, Long Island, to work in the bond business and rents a modest house next to the mysterious mansion of Jay Gatsby. There, he reconnects with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, wealthy East Eggers whose opulent life masks deep moral decay—Tom’s racism and infidelity, Daisy’s cynical detachment, and Jordan Baker’s dishonesty. Nick is drawn into their world, but it is Gatsby who captivates him: a self-made millionaire whose lavish parties mask an intense, quiet longing. Through Jordan Baker, Nick learns that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be near Daisy, the woman he loved five years earlier as a young officer in Louisville, and that he has spent years crafting an elaborate persona—Oxford graduate, war hero, aristocrat—to win her back. Nick agrees to arrange a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, reigniting their romance and exposing the fragility of Gatsby’s dream.

As Gatsby and Daisy rekindle their relationship, tensions rise with Tom Buchanan, who grows suspicious and eventually confronts Gatsby in a brutal showdown at the Plaza Hotel. Tom dismantles Gatsby’s fabricated identity, revealing his criminal ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and exposing the source of his wealth as bootlegging. Daisy, unable to fully renounce Tom or declare she never loved him, shatters Gatsby’s idealized vision of their past. That same afternoon, Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy but owned by Gatsby. In the aftermath, Tom manipulates George Wilson, Myrtle’s widower, into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer. Meanwhile, Gatsby, still guarding Daisy’s house in the moonlight, refuses to leave, convinced he can protect her from blame. Nick, increasingly disillusioned by the East’s moral emptiness, watches as Gatsby’s world collapses around him, even as those who benefited from his hospitality vanish without a word.

After Gatsby is shot and killed by George Wilson—who then turns the gun on himself—Nick struggles to organize a funeral for a man whose wealth and fame meant nothing to those who once flocked to his parties. Only Gatsby’s father, a humble Midwesterner who cherished his son’s ambition, and a few others attend. Nick confronts Jordan Baker, who dismisses his moral outrage, and encounters Tom Buchanan, who coldly admits he told Wilson about Gatsby’s car, justifying it as self-preservation. Haunted by the emptiness of Gatsby’s dream and the callousness of the wealthy, Nick leaves New York, realizing that people like Tom and Daisy are 'careless' people who smash things and retreat into their money. In his final reflection on the beach, Nick sees the green light at the end of Daisy’s dock as a symbol of the American Dream—endlessly pursued, always just out of reach, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
